analysis.one_liner: Raises required fuel economy for new cars and light trucks by 20%, then 40%, over the next decade.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in April 1991, but it never received a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required each automaker to make its car and light truck fleets 20 percent more fuel-efficient by model year 1996 and 40 percent more efficient by 2001, compared with its 1988 fleet, with limits set by the Transportation Secretary. It would also have covered light trucks — pickups, vans and jeeps — under strict legislative standards for the first time, doubled fines for repeat violators, and required better consumer information and studies of future standards. The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee and sat on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and households that buy gasoline: the bill's findings cite expert estimates that fleet fuel economy of 38 to 45 miles per gallon was achievable with existing technology, and project that a 20 percent improvement by 1996 and 40 percent by 2001 would save 2.5 million barrels of oil per day by 2005 [S4]. The bill also cites past improvements that saved drivers at least $40 billion [S4]. Reduced oil dependence and lower carbon dioxide emissions (about 440 million tons per year by 2005 under the bill's estimates) benefit the public broadly [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Requires each manufacturer's passenger car fleet to reach 1988 fuel economy plus 20 percent by model years 1996-2000 (between 27.5 and 40 mpg) and plus 40 percent by 2001 (between 33 and 45 mpg), with similar percentage increases for light trucks [S4].

Applies strict, legislatively set standards to light trucks — small pickups, vans and jeeps — which by 1991 were about one-third of new passenger vehicle sales but had never been held to strict standards and whose fuel economy had not improved in a decade [S4].
Doubles civil penalties for manufacturers that repeatedly violate the standard and adjusts penalties for inflation, giving the standard enforcement teeth [S4].
Requires EPA to study annually whether official fuel economy test results match what real drivers actually get, and to report to Congress, so buyers are not misled by optimistic window stickers [S4].
Directs the Secretary of Energy to distribute at least 100 explanatory fuel economy booklets each year to every car dealer [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers bear the cost of engineering and retooling to meet the higher standards, and face doubled fines for repeat violations; some of that cost would likely reach vehicle buyers as higher sticker prices. Makers of the least-efficient fleets, particularly large pickups and vans, faced the largest changes, and the oil industry faced lower domestic gasoline demand [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Automakers, truck-heavy fleets, and vehicle buyers

drawbacks.text: Higher fuel economy requirements typically raise the upfront price of new vehicles, and buyers who do not drive many miles may never recover that cost in fuel savings [S4].

The percentage-based formula requires every manufacturer — including those already selling efficient small cars — to improve by the same proportion from its 1988 fleet, which the bill defends as necessary but which gives manufacturers with less room to improve less flexibility [S4].
The Secretary of Transportation could modify standards downward through a rulemaking process after petitions, introducing regulatory uncertainty into targets the bill itself sets [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's own findings argue the savings historically outweighed the costs — efficiency gains between 1973 and 1987 saved drivers at least $40 billion — and assert feasible improvements were possible with existing technology without changing vehicle size or performance [S4]. An honest reading must acknowledge that buyers would pay more for new vehicles upfront and that the claims about low-cost technological feasibility were estimates by agencies and experts, not guarantees; the bill's flexibility for downward modification partly reflects that uncertainty [S4].

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill favorably in April 1991 and it was placed on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Introduced January 29, 1991 by Senator Bryan with 36 cosponsors, and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S6].
The Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer held hearings on February 21, 1991 (S.Hrg. 102-19) [S6].

The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with amendments on March 19, 1991, and Senator Hollings reported it to the Senate on April 25, 1991, with written report No. 102-48; additional and minority views were filed [S6].
On April 25, 1991 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 75) [S6].
A star print was ordered May 7, 1991; after that the record shows no further action, no floor debate, and no vote, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. automakers and the oil industry were better off, because no higher fuel economy mandate ever reached a vote; drivers continued to bear the fuel costs and emissions the bill was written to reduce [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start: of its 36 cosponsors, 28 were Democrats and 8 were Republicans, and the committee reported it favorably, though minority views were filed [S5][S6].

industries.note: The bill would have forced every automaker to make its car and light truck fleets 20 percent, then 40 percent, more efficient than its 1988 fleet, with doubled fines for repeat violations [S4]. Light trucks — a large and profitable segment — would have been brought under strict legislative standards for the first time, so the industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against drivers' fuel savings [S4].
The bill projects that a 20 percent efficiency gain by 1996 and 40 percent by 2001 would cut U.S. oil use by 2.5 million barrels per day by 2005, reducing domestic gasoline demand [S4].

Dealers face marginally more administrative burden but the bill requires the Energy Department to supply each dealer at least 100 consumer fuel economy booklets per year at no indication of cost to the dealer [S4].
